name: Russian as spoken in Latvia
variety: Russian as used in Latvia. Native speakers in Latvia use the sound system of Standard Russian; regional phonetic differences are slight and little documented. The description below is therefore that of Standard Russian. Russian spoken as a second language by Latvian speakers differs more, and that accent is what the eSpeak NG voice imitates.
sources: Yanushevskaya, Irena & Bunčić, Daniel (2015). Russian. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 45(2), 221-228.
Jones, Daniel & Ward, Dennis (1969). The Phonetics of Russian. Cambridge University Press.
Avanesov, R. I. (1984). Russkoe literaturnoe proiznošenie. Moscow: Prosveščenie.
Timberlake, Alan (2004). A Reference Grammar of Russian. Cambridge University Press.
Fant, Gunnar (1960). Acoustic Theory of Speech Production. The Hague: Mouton.
Ringen, Catherine & Kulikov, Vladimir (2012). Voicing in Russian stops: cross-linguistic implications. Journal of Slavic Linguistics 20(2), 269-300.
Bryzgunova, E. A. (1977). Zvuki i intonacija russkoj reči. Moscow: Russkij jazyk.
Laua, Alise (1997). Latviešu literārās valodas fonētika. Rīga: Zvaigzne ABC. (for the Latvian sound system behind the accent features)

vowel_formants.speaker: adult male, single speaker of Standard Russian, sustained isolated vowels; no measurements of speakers from Latvia are known to me

contrasts: palatalised ('soft') versus non-palatalised ('hard') consonants at almost every place and manner, also word-finally and before consonants
voiced versus voiceless obstruents (prevoiced versus voiceless unaspirated)
five stressed vowels /i e a o u/, with [ɨ] after hard consonants
position of stress is lexically contrastive
long /ɕː/ and geminates at morpheme boundaries
allophony: akanye: unstressed /o/ and /a/ merge after hard consonants, [ɐ] in the first pretonic syllable and [ə] elsewhere
ikanye: unstressed /e/, /a/, /o/ after soft consonants merge as [ɪ]
stressed vowels are fronted next to soft consonants ([æ], [ɵ], [ʉ])
word-final obstruents are devoiced; obstruent clusters take the voicing of their last member
/ɫ/ is dental and velarised; /r/ is an apical trill or tap
phonotactics: onset and coda clusters of up to four consonants
no voiced obstruents before a pause
only reduced vowel qualities in unstressed syllables

stress.rule: Stress can fall on any syllable and may shift within a paradigm; it is not shown in ordinary spelling except by ё.
stress.cues: duration and vowel quality first, then intensity

rhythm.vowel_reduction: strong, as in Standard Russian (akanye and ikanye)
rhythm.notes: No rhythm measurements for speakers from Latvia are cited here.

length.notes: No phonemic vowel length. Long /ɕː/ and geminates at morpheme boundaries.

voice_onset_time_ms.source: Ringen & Kulikov 2012 (monolingual speakers of Standard Russian, not speakers from Latvia)

intonation.declarative: fall on the stressed syllable of the nuclear word, low afterwards (IK-1)
intonation.yes_no_question: steep rise on the stressed syllable of the word in focus, then low (IK-3); no final rise
intonation.wh_question: high or falling accent on the question word or nucleus, then falling to low (IK-2)
intonation.continuation: rise on the last stressed syllable of the non-final phrase
intonation.accent_shape: statement nucleus: fall within the stressed syllable; question nucleus: late-peaked rise followed by a low tail
intonation.notes: Described for Standard Russian; no study of intonation in Latvian Russian is cited.

tone.notes: No lexical tone or pitch accent.

problems: The voice models a Latvian accent rather than native Russian as spoken in Latvia: the phoneme table ru-lv (inherits ru) and the ?2 rules remove features that native speakers in Latvia share with the standard.
Unstressed е stays [e] (река [rʲeˈka], сегодня [sʲeˈvodɲʌ]): no ikanye. а, я after soft consonants stay [a] as in ru.
Unstressed о keeps the phoneme o (молоко is output as [moloˈko]) and is realised with an open vowel (formant file aa_7): one degree of akanye, without the [ə] of other unstressed syllables.
Hard л is a clear alveolar [l] (the Latvian-style l), not velarised [ɫ].
Final б and в are not devoiced (хлеб [xlʲeb], лев [lʲev]); final д, г, ж, з are.
щ is a long hard [ʃʃ] and сч is [ʃ] instead of soft [ɕː].
Soft н is the palatal nasal [ɲ] (kept word-finally: день [dʲeɲ]); soft л is l plus glide and is lost word-finally as in ru; м and з before soft vowels can stay hard (мил [mil], земля [zemlʲˈa]).
ь and ъ before я, ю, е, ё give a short pause (семья [sʲem_ˈja]).

Voice settings copy the Latvian and Latgalian voices (speed 95, stressLength and stressAmp with small stressed-unstressed differences, 'words 0 2' pause between a vowel-final and a vowel-initial word), which weakens the stress-timed rhythm of Russian.
As in ru: stress from the ru dictionary or guessed; no voicing assimilation between preposition and host; default eSpeak tunes only.
good: uses the large Russian stress dictionary
regressive voicing assimilation inside words (вокзал, отдать)
[ɨ] after hard consonants including жи, ши, ци
soft нь is kept distinct word-finally

notes: I know of no published phonetic description of Russian in Latvia that could be cited with confidence, so no variety-specific numbers are given; the numeric blocks repeat Standard Russian data and are marked low confidence for this variety. The voice was contributed by the maintainer of the Latvian voice (voice file header).
